items.title: The 2027 Chief Claims Officer
items.original_title: The 2027 Chief Claims Officer
items.rss_title: The 2027 Chief Claims Officer
items.rss_description: The 2027 Chief Claims Officer Claims ITL Editorial Team Tue, 10/06/2026 - 11:19 Chief claims officers must transform their departments into AI-native ground-truth engines or risk becoming the bottleneck in enterprise transformation. October 7, 2026 Image For decades, the mandate of the chief claims cfficer was relatively clear: build a strong organization to investigate claims, control costs, manage litigation, negotiate settlements, and deliver fair outcomes. That mandate is no longer sufficient. The 2027 chief claims officer has a much bigger job: build the insurer's ground-truth engine—an AI-native operation that produces superior outcomes, industrializes negotiation excellence, and converts what claims learns into intelligence for the entire enterprise. This is not simply about using AI to make legacy claims processes more efficient. AI is turning insurance into an information business—and the most important ground truth in that business is generated in claims. Claims reveal what actually happened to the risks the insurer underwrote, what drove the loss, and what ultimately determined its economic outcome. To compete in an AI world, insurers will need to capture that ground truth, make it machine-readable, and use it to improve underwriting, pricing, reserving, and portfolio management. That puts claims—and the chief claims officer—on the front line of this unprecedented transformation. A new competitive environment Claims officers in traditional claims organizations face urgent and pressing competition from two sources at once. On one side is an increasingly industrialized plaintiff bar. On the other side is a new generation of AI-native insurers, poised to move forward. On the first side, consider Morgan & Morgan. The personal-injury giant says it has invested roughly $300 million in technology and AI and plans at least $1 billion more over the next decade. Its proprietary MX2 platform supports medical-record extraction, case research, document generation, demand letters, and trial preparation, while Injury.com digitally acquires and qualifies potential claims. Private equity is adding fuel, investing in personal-injury platforms to scale technology, analytics, marketing and standardized operations. The plaintiff bar is turning claim development and negotiation from individual craftsmanship into an industrial system. On the second side, a new generation of AI-native insurers is being built without decades of legacy technology, workflows and organizational baggage. Companies such as Corgi are attempting to build insurance businesses from inception around modern data architectures, AI agents and technology-speed iteration. McKinsey has warned that AI-native insurance businesses can increasingly build and refine products in weeks while incumbents remain calibrated to annual planning cycles and multi-year transformations. Legacy insurers are being squeezed from both directions: out-innovated by the plaintiff bar in the contest over outcomes and potentially out-architected by AI-native insurers in the contest over how insurance itself operates. Claims sits directly in the middle. That changes the requirements of its leader. 1. Level the playing field with the plaintiff bar The plaintiff bar has largely approached AI as a weapon for improving economic outcomes. Carriers have largely approached it as a tool for workflow efficiency. AI-powered demand packages are working. Carriers are only beginning to experiment seriously with the corresponding AI-powered offer package. Meanwhile, sophisticated plaintiff organizations are accumulating data, developing proprietary AI and attracting enormous capital. The plaintiff bar is both the threat and the proof point. They are investing their own money—and increasing institutional capital—because better case development, persuasion, and negotiation improve their economics. The CCO must build institutional capabilities that can match increasingly industrialized counterparties. 2. Institutionalize negotiation excellence Most carriers have some excellent negotiators. That is no longer enough. If negotiation materially affects indemnity outcomes, it cannot remain an individual skill distributed unevenly across thousands of claims professionals. The organization should know who its elite negotiators are, why they outperform and how those behaviors can be replicated. Carriers that cannot identify, measure and reproduce negotiation excellence do not really possess a negotiation capability. They possess individual negotiators. The CCO must turn individual excellence into measurable institutional capability. 3. Stop putting AI band-aids on pre-AI claims operations Many carriers can produce an impressive list of AI-centric projects: summarize a file, extract information, draft correspondence, analyze a demand, route work, search notes, or give adjusters Copilot. Those applications can create real value. But old process plus an AI tool means slightly better old process. McKinsey has warned about layering new technology onto legacy insurance operating models. BCG similarly distinguishes between deploying AI into existing processes and reshaping workflows around AI. The CCO must redesign the operating model, not merely automate the existing one. 4. Build machine-first claims The traditional claim file was built primarily for humans. Documents, notes, emails, medical records, and litigation materials accumulate while experienced professionals gradually construct an understanding of what happened. In an AI-native operation, every claim should progressively become a machine-readable representation of the claim—the people, events, evidence, injuries, allegations, relationships, negotiations and outcomes. That structured claim becomes the substrate on which specialized AI agents can continuously reason. Instead of occasionally asking AI to summarize a file, machines continuously read, structure, monitor, compare, detect, and prepare. The CCO must make claims machine-readable while elevating, not diminishing, human judgment and action. 5. Build and lead a hybrid workforce The future claim officer will have two kinds of capacity at their disposal: human expertise and machine intelligence. AI agents will increasingly read, structure, monitor, research, compare, detect, analyze and prepare. Humans will increasingly concentrate on judgment, investigation, strategy, creativity, empathy, supervision, accountability and negotiation. That will make exceptional claims professionals more important, not less. Imagine an elite negotiator supported by agents that continuously understand the evidence, medical history, venue, plaintiff counsel, negotiation history, and comparable outcomes. The machine handles much of the cognitive preparation. The human concentrates on what exceptional humans do best: think, strategize, persuade, read the counterparty, exercise judgment, and negotiate. The CCO must become the architect of human and machine capacity—designing how each works together to produce better outcomes. 6. Make every negotiation a learning event A sophisticated plaintiff demand should eventually meet an equally sophisticated carrier response. But the bigger opportunity comes afterward. Every demand, analysis, strategy, offer, response, counteroffer, and outcome must become institutional knowledge in the same way that the plaintiff bar is institutionalizing these events. Which plaintiff firms consistently outperform? Which strategies work against them? Which facts change settlement value? Which negotiators outperform expectations? Where does the organization systematically overpay? Every negotiation should make the next negotiation smarter. The CCO must ensure every claim and negotiation makes the organization smarter. 7. Elevate claims into the insurer's ground-truth engine This is where the transformation extends beyond claims. Underwriting begins with hypotheses about risk. Pricing quantifies them. Reserving updates them. Claims discovers what was actually true. Claims learns what caused the loss, how injuries developed, what evidence mattered, how attorneys behaved, which defenses and negotiation strategies worked, and what the risk ultimately cost. Yet much of that knowledge remains trapped in PDFs, notes, litigation files and the heads of experienced claims professionals. Claims should continuously produce structured intelligence that flows into underwriting, pricing, reserving, risk, reinsurance and portfolio management. The claim is no longer simply something to resolve and close. It is one of the insurer's richest proprietary information assets. The CCO must turn claims knowledge into enterprise intelligence—making the claims organization the feedback loop that allows the entire enterprise to learn. 8. Don't let claims become the transformation bottleneck This may be the requirement that matters most to the rest of the C-suite. A legacy insurer can modernize distribution, underwriting, pricing and portfolio management. But if its richest source of ground truth remains trapped inside a document-centric, human-first claims operation moving through multi-year transformation cycles, the rest of the enterprise eventually hits a wall. AI-native competitors do not have to unwind decades of organizational architecture before redesigning how humans, machines and data work together. Incumbents do. That makes speed itself a competitive capability. The modern CCO must protect the integrity of a massive, consequential operation while simultaneously making it capable of continuous change. The plaintiff bar is moving at technology speed. AI-native competitors are being built for technology speed. Claims cannot continue moving at insurance speed. The CCO must ensure claims leads rather than constrains the insurer's AI transformation. The mandate has changed None of these requirements eliminates the traditional responsibilities of the CCO. Claims still must be handled fairly; customers, regulatory obligations, litigation, reserves and operational discipline still matter. But those responsibilities are increasingly table stakes. Sophisticated plaintiff organizations are industrializing the pursuit of settlement dollars while AI-native insurers are being architected as technology-speed information businesses. Between them sits a claims organization that, at many incumbents, was designed for another era. That creates both a threat and an extraordinary opportunity. Carriers that generate that ground truth better, negotiate from it more effectively, make it machine-readable and distribute it throughout the enterprise will possess something more valuable than a more efficient claims department. They will possess a continuously learning insurance enterprise. As chief claims officers enter 2027, the question is no longer whether their departments will use more AI. It is whether they can transform their departments into a competitive advantage rather than the bottleneck preventing the enterprise from changing with it. Taylor Smith John Burge

items.rss_description: Gen Z Drives Insurance Claims Transformation Customer Experience ITL Editorial Team Wed, 10/14/2026 - 13:12 Gen Z's demand for instant digital experiences is forcing insurers to modernize claims payments or risk losing policyholders. October 15, 2026 Image As digital natives who've grown up tethered to smartphones and social media, the Gen Z population's effect on today's consumer trends is well documented . Young shoppers' demands for instant gratification in consumer transactions have ushered in an era of in-app shopping, next-day shipping, and fast, friction-free digital payment options. Gen Z's influence is extending to the insurance claims process, as well. More and more, Gen Z's preferences are pushing the industry to uplevel its claims experience – to make it faster, more convenient, more tied to mobile, and more transparent to the policyholder. InvoiceCloud's 2026 Claims Experience survey of 1,000 U.S. policyholders shows Gen Z is nearly twice as likely as the overall population to prefer a digital wallet for claims payments (13% versus 7%). Recent research shines a light on policyholders' discontent with what they identify as their biggest deal breaker: an unacceptably slow process for paying claims. The InvoiceCloud survey found that only 9% of policyholders received their claims payment within two days. Meanwhile, a quarter of respondents say it took more than a week to receive their claims payout, while an unfortunate 13% waited "several weeks" to get these urgent funds. This could cause ripple effects. In a 2022 report, " Transforming claims and underwriting with AI ", Accenture estimated that poor claims experiences could put up to $170 billion in global insurance premiums at risk through 2027. The InvoiceCloud survey shows how these risks could materialize. At least 75% of policyholders surveyed say they would consider switching carriers after a single negative claims experience. That's a high percentage in any field, but it's particularly high in personal-lines P&C, where switching providers is often easier than it is in commercial, E&S, or other specialty markets. Improving the claims process How do insurance carriers improve the claims process? Our research found that speed and transparency matter most of all to policyholders. When asked directly, 30% named a faster claims payment after approval as the single change they want most, more than any other option, while 22% preferred clearer status communication. Gen Z echoes that second point: 24% named clearer, more consistent communication about payment status as the one change they would make, on par with the 21% who named faster payment. Another issue: Many carriers have modernized inbound premium payments, but outbound disbursements still rely on paper checks and manual processing. Paper checks create fraud risk, delivery problems, and extra work for commissions and return premiums. The next generation of policyholders is demanding two changes to this payment structure. They prefer a shift to digital, and they want choices. Digital disbursement platforms can support a wide variety of options including ACH/direct deposit, debit cards, virtual cards, and digital wallets. Direct deposit to a bank account is policyholders' favorite payout, preferred by 52% of respondents, more than all other options combined. Printed checks still account for 19%, likely reflecting legacy carrier processes rather than genuine preference. The gap between generations is wide: 32% of Baby Boomers prefer a printed check, compared with just 9% of Gen Z. If slow payouts can lead to defections, digital insurance payments can operate as a retention tool. Insurance carriers can do this by ensuring this critical touchpoint becomes an easy experience end-to-end, from allowing policyholders to self-serve through digital premium payments, paperless billing, and automatic payments, to instant disbursements delivered however policyholders prefer to receive funds. Real-time digital disbursements are funds sent electronically and received quickly, without a paper check in the middle. For insurance carriers, this means agent commissions and return premiums move through digital payment processing solutions rather than the mail. More importantly, it means getting funds into policyholders' hands fast, when it matters the most. Raising expectations As younger policyholders account for a larger share of the insurance market, experiences they've grown accustomed to in other walks of life will increasingly become expectations for insurance as well. For many, this translates to being able to complete more transactions on smartphones. Digital payments enable customers to choose a payment method from their phone, receive payment notifications, track payment status, access transaction details, and receive funds directly into an eligible account or wallet. That matters most to the youngest policyholders. When asked for the easiest way to access funds in an emergency, 19% of Gen Z chose a mobile wallet, compared with 5% of Baby Boomers, while only 9% would withdraw cash at a bank, compared with 34% of Baby Boomers. Gen Z's imprint on insurance claims is becoming more pronounced. Today's policyholders want to have insurance claims processed and paid out faster. But they want more. They want the entire journey – culminating in how and when they get paid – to feel as immediate and seamless as any other digital financial transaction. Ray Walsh

items.title: Turning Volatility Into Value
items.original_title: Turning Volatility Into Value
items.rss_title: Turning Volatility Into Value
items.rss_description: Turning Volatility Into Value Underwriting RyanMeyer Wed, 10/14/2026 - 10:37 Amid today's heightened uncertainty, Dawn Miller, chief commercial officer at Lloyd's, explores how insurers can innovate their way to value both for themselves and for their clients. October 14, 2026 Image Paul Carroll We’re in an exceptionally volatile period, with major geopolitical and economic risks on top of climate-driven catastrophes, nuclear verdicts, and more. The International Insurance Society’s annual Global Insurance Forum in November, which you’re sponsoring and hosting at Lloyd’s, has as its theme this year: "Turning Volatility Into Value." How do we do that? Dawn Miller I'm just coming off some time at CIAB [Council of Insurance Agents and Brokers] in Colorado, and the topic that is on everyone's mind, in addition to market conditions, is how multiple perils are intersecting with global trends to create an increasingly varied and complex risk landscape, with some risks well modeled and others less so. In the past, our market would focus on certain CAT risks, certain natural perils happening in one place at one time. Now we're seeing multiple risks interact at the same time, from natural catastrophes and supply-chain disruption to inflation, geopolitical uncertainty and demographic risks. And those are just to name a few. It’s the interaction among these different risks that is adding new layers of complexity. We have innovations that allow us to model with more transparency, and we can bring in supplementary models to assess risk. That's a good thing. But it takes an enormous amount of creativity to predict the layers of complexity around us today. Paul Carroll Yes, some people who’ve written for us refer to a “polycrisis.” You mention modeling. Is that the main way insurers make sense of all these complicated connections, or is it improvements in scenario planning, or something else? Dawn Miller I believe it's multiple things. We're seeing innovations in modeling—additional data transparency being plugged into some of those core models that we've always used to look at some known perils. The perils aren't changing, but our ability to understand them is getting better, sometimes dramatically. There's also an opportunity for geopolitical assessments, economic assessments, and social demographic assessments to all play a role. The modeling itself is a bit of a Rubik's Cube with multiple facets to it. Paul Carroll Wall Street talks a lot about alpha and embraces volatility because it creates opportunities. Historically, insurers have not liked volatility. How do you change that thinking? Dawn Miller Given that Lloyd’s is guiding a marketplace, we're creating the conditions for success for the world's best risk takers to attach the risks they want to underwrite with capital. We see a mix in our marketplace. We do see investors coming in looking for some of that volatility. That’s what they like, and it fits as a diversifier into their portfolios. We see others wanting the longer-tail risk. This may not be as volatile, but they want it for their own investment reasons. Our role is to create the environment for all those different profiles to exist and to all benefit from the diversification of our marketplace. It's not an either-or—the alpha seekers or the beta seekers. It's having both in an environment where they can coexist. Paul Carroll Volatility requires agility not just for those transacting in your marketplace but for you, too. How is Lloyd's getting faster at identifying opportunities and scaling the winners as quickly as possible? Dawn Miller In March, we launched our new five-year strategy, Advance and protect. It is designed to sharpen Lloyd’s financial edge and maximize our unique capital advantage, including by creating a more efficient and flexible marketplace by making the platform more investable, clear, transparent and agile. Right now, there's some additional reporting, different ways of working, maybe some duplicated oversight here and there—things that have grown up over time for all the right intentions, but maybe as we evolve are not as pragmatic any more. All of those cause a little bit of extra cost, whether it's in time or resources, because time is money at the end of the day. So we're making things much clearer, making it much more cost-efficient, making sure we are an engine for driving new talent into the marketplace, attracting the best talent and then recycling them back out as advocates and having the marketplace stronger for their being with us. You're creating an ecosystem that is the center of attracting the world's best risk takers, the best capital together with the best brokers, best clients, the best risk. What that gives us is the ability to innovate. When we think about Lloyd's and the underpinnings of our strategy, our superpower is our capital diversification benefits. Our other superpowers are around our license structure, the framework we have for innovation, the ability to syndicate risk rapidly, our very strong financial strength ratings. Innovation, whether it is the birth of a new product, or the birth of a new structure, or how we deal with some of the extreme large-scale infrastructure, energy, supply chain, and transportation issues that we see around the world—that is going to take more than one mind to solve. And we are the marketplace for that sort of solution creation. Paul Carroll At ITL, in our little way, our mantra is: Nobody is as smart as everybody. Dawn Miller That's exactly right. Our role is to convene a marketplace, creating those conditions for success. It happened 338 years ago when people came together over a cup of coffee and said, Let's share this risk so we can get these ships across the globe. Today, the same principle of combining expertise and capital continues across the underwriting room, Lloyd’s Lab and Lloyd’s Academy. Paul Carroll I’m glad you mentioned the lab and the academy, because, as an old hand on innovation efforts, I wanted to ask how they fit into your broader innovation ecosystem. Dawn Miller Absolutely. As you know, Lloyd's Lab launched in 2018 to make sure we had a place to accelerate—not necessarily incubate, and I want to make that distinction—new risk-taking ideas or risk-servicing ideas. Over time, we've grown to have about 160 alumni. This past cohort, Cohort 17, just went through a selection process. We received 280 applications from 31 countries. Fifteen companies were invited to pitch to the market, and 10 were selected for the 10-week Accelerator program. The market plays a central role in that selection process because the Lab is designed to respond to real market needs. The focus of Cohort 17 has been in areas where the Lloyd’s market is actively seeking solutions that improve how the market operates day to day to strengthen its ability to respond to the complexity of today’s risk landscape and this can be seen through the themes: operational efficiency, new products and experimental innovation. What does that mean? They come in at all different stages of businesses and ideas. They have mentors from the marketplace. They hone, shift, and massage their product and their service. Then they exit the other end, generally about 80 to 85% of them, with either capacity for a proof of concept or a service contract or service proof of concept into the marketplace. That ranges from new products—cloud downtime, wildfire, data analytics—to a whole variety of services. They work their way through the market, with an accelerated cover holder process. Some of them, like Parsyl, started in the Lloyd’s Lab. Parsyl began by using data and technology to tackle risks in global health supply chains, then became a Syndicate-in-a-Box and now has in-principle approval to become a full syndicate. That’s the process of taking innovation, testing and proving it in the market, and ultimately giving it the opportunity to scale. They're a part of our ecosystem once they come out as alumni, and they stay within our ecosystem around the world. We continue to help by giving them opportunities to be exposed to end clients, to regulators, to investors, etc. Paul Carroll How do you expect these topics—including innovation, geopolitical risk, and emerging technologies—to be developed at the Global Insurance Forum? Dawn Miller I always look forward to the Global Insurance Forum; it's a place where market leaders and market practitioners are coming together to exchange on an equal level. We’re reflecting the trends of the times, whether that’s private credit, scaling innovation or how we move beyond the tactical. This year’s theme, “Turning volatility into value,” really captures that. It’s about moving beyond reacting to uncertainty and using better insight, specialist expertise and flexible capital to anticipate changing needs, build solutions and give customers the confidence to invest and grow. The companies that come together are from all around the world. Everybody's lens is going to have a slightly different take on how they deal with geopolitical risk or how they're dealing with supply chain or how they're dealing with credit risk or what they're facing at that exact moment. Bringing all of that together allows us to create a narrative that firmly implants how our industry is driving resilience forward. Our industry provides the oxygen for the economies around us. And I believe we allow our industry to represent itself or be represented by others in a way other than that. I wish we talked more about the outcome our industry enables: resilience. We need to explain insurance through communities, businesses and economies it enables to recover and thrive and persist. The forum also creates a great opportunity to bring some of our young leaders to the table. Their perspectives are varied and rich, and we need that diversity of thought. Paul Carroll As someone who’s covered technology innovations for decades, I confess that it was only about 15 years ago that I realized that none of that happens without insurance. Every major innovation—the personal computer, the internet, the smartphone, social media, search engines, GPS, the driverless car—comes with risks, and nobody can take those risks without some sort of protection. Dawn Miller Right. Isn't it funny? We all sort of take it for granted. If we could just reframe the conversation and talk more clearly about how insurance creates resilient communities, helping them thrive, we would give people a much better understanding of the value our industry provides. At Lloyd’s, we don’t just seek to understand risk, we take it on, bringing together expertise, capital and risk appetite to help businesses move forward. The issue couldn't be more important than it is right now, with the multiple layers of risks that surround us. Paul Carroll Thanks, Dawn. It’s always great talking with you. Dawn Miller Thank you for having me, Paul; always a pleasure. If you’re interested in attending the Global Insurance Forum, you can register here. Insurance Thought Leadership

items.title: Why Are Insurance Jobs Disappearing?
items.original_title: Why Are Insurance Jobs Disappearing?
items.rss_title: Why Are Insurance Jobs Disappearing?
items.rss_description: Why Are Insurance Jobs Disappearing? PaulCarroll Mon, 10/05/2026 - 17:40 The employment report for September in the U.S. showed a loss of 7,000 jobs in financial services. Insurance, alone, has now lost 90,000 jobs since May 2025. What's going on? I have a theory, and it's not about artificial intelligence. If I'm right, hiring in insurance will stay in the doldrums for a while. Let's have a look. As Insurance Business reports , the industry still employs a massive 2.9 million people in the U.S., but claims jobs are down a hefty 21% over the past year, while life and health is off 4%, P&C down 1.7%, and agents and brokers down 1.1%. The losses are accelerating: The article says, " Insurers lost about 1,900 jobs a month on average in 2025 and roughly 6,900 a month so far in 2026." A thorough analysis in Barron's mostly attributes the job losses to cost-cutting under pressure. Barron's notes that the surge in rates following the COVID disruption has slowed. In addition, government subsidies for healthcare have been cut even as claims costs keep increasing. In the face of pressure on both premiums and expenses, insurers have had to become more efficient, Barron's says. It does say AI has played a role by automating tasks but doesn't treat that as a huge issue just yet (and I've been arguing for months that the fears of job losses to AI are overstated). You could also add the effects of the "silver tsunami" -- the oft-quoted projection by the Bureau of Labor Statistics in 2021 that 400,000 insurance professionals would retire by the end of 2026. Unemployment in insurance remains well below that for the economy writ large -- 3.1%, vs. 4.2% -- so some of the job losses may simply be that companies haven't yet been able to fill the positions left by retirements. But I think there's an overarching issue that gets short shrift if you spend too much time in the details. My Theory My theory boils down to uncertainty. I think economic and geopolitical uncertainty are holding back the economy, in general, and the insurance industry, in particular. And I don't see the uncertainty subsiding any time soon. Tariffs have not only raised costs but, because of their on-again, off-again nature, have slowed investment and the sort of adaptation of supply chains that would ordinarily happen if, say, Canadian lumber suddenly became 50% more expensive. Why spend a lot of money and time if prices might return to normal shortly, whether because of a court ruling against tariffs, because Democrats win control of Congress and assert its power, or simply because President Trump changed his mind? Now add the uncertainty from the war on Iran. Even though oil flows out of the Middle East are improving, Iran retains the capability to attack tankers, to blow up one of the major pipelines being used to skirt the Strait of Hormuz, or to do more damage to the diesel refineries in the region, whose loss has contributed so much to the soaring prices for the crucial fuel. While Trump has repeatedly told us that Iran wants to make a deal and that prices for oil will soon plummet, some of us are old enough to remember how the Iranian zealots acted after taking 66 American hostages in 1979. Angry at President Carter, they didn't release the hostages until minutes after Ronald Reagan became president in January 1981. Who's to say the Iranian theocrats won't treat Trump the way their predecessors treated Carter, declining to make a deal until he leaves office? What is now looking like a blue wave in next month's midterm elections might relieve some of the uncertainty about tariffs, perhaps even leading to serious settlement talks with Iran, but a loss of control by Trump would surely lead to at least a burst of chaos -- perhaps even a sustained stretch. The Democrats are itching to go after him, and he would surely return fire with every one of the many assets at his disposal. The current uncertainty and the prospects that it will continue will create headwinds for the economy, which insurance, especially P&C, tracks closely. The problem will be even worse than normal, I believe, because the effects will hit personal lines so hard. Replacement costs for cars have surged in recent years because of supply chain disruptions, and they will likely stay in flux. Insurers will also have to deal with possibly significant changes in driver behavior if gasoline and diesel prices stay so high -- or go even higher. Costs for home repairs have likewise soared, and uncertainty will tend to keep them high. Meanwhile, the general uncertainty about the economy has fueled inflation, leading the Fed to raise rates for the first time in years and to signal that it may raise rates again soon. A result has been 7% mortgages that have pretty much crushed the housing sector. The reduction in construction means fewer homes to insure, and the stagnant resale market limits the opportunities to poach customers as homes change hands. The result will, I believe, be unrelenting pressure on revenue and costs at a time when customers are exhausted from all the post-COVID rate increases. I hope I'm wrong, but it's hard to see a lot of hiring in that sort of environment. Cheers, Paul Image Paul Carroll The latest jobs report for the U.S. highlighted a surprising decline in employment in insurance. I have a theory about the reason -- and it's not AI. Unemployment in insurance remains well below that for the economy writ large -- 3.1%, vs. 4.2% -- so some of the job losses may simply be that companies haven't yet been able to fill the positions left by retirements. But I think there's an overarching issue that gets short shrift if you spend too much time in the details. My Theory My theory boils down to uncertainty. I think economic and geopolitical uncertainty are holding back the economy, in general, and the insurance industry, in particular. And I don't see the uncertainty subsiding any time soon. Tariffs have not only raised costs but, because of their on-again, off-again nature, have slowed investment and the sort of adaptation of supply chains that would ordinarily happen if, say, Canadian lumber suddenly became 50% more expensive. Why spend a lot of money and time if prices might return to normal shortly, whether because of a court ruling against tariffs, because Democrats win control of Congress and assert its power, or simply because President Trump changed his mind? Now add the uncertainty from the war on Iran. Even though oil flows out of the Middle East are improving, Iran retains the capability to attack tankers, to blow up one of the major pipelines being used to skirt the Strait of Hormuz, or to do more damage to the diesel refineries in the region, whose loss has contributed so much to the soaring prices for the crucial fuel. While Trump has repeatedly told us that Iran wants to make a deal and that prices for oil will soon plummet, some of us are old enough to remember how the Iranian zealots acted after taking 66 American hostages in 1979. Angry at President Carter, they didn't release the hostages until minutes after Ronald Reagan became president in January 1981. Who's to say the Iranian theocrats won't treat Trump the way their predecessors treated Carter, declining to make a deal until he leaves office? What is now looking like a blue wave in next month's midterm elections might relieve some of the uncertainty about tariffs, perhaps even leading to serious settlement talks with Iran, but a loss of control by Trump would surely lead to at least a burst of chaos -- perhaps even a sustained stretch. The Democrats are itching to go after him, and he would surely return fire with every one of the many assets at his disposal. The current uncertainty and the prospects that it will continue will create headwinds for the economy, which insurance, especially P&C, tracks closely. The problem will be even worse than normal, I believe, because the effects will hit personal lines so hard. Replacement costs for cars have surged in recent years because of supply chain disruptions, and they will likely stay in flux. Insurers will also have to deal with possibly significant changes in driver behavior if gasoline and diesel prices stay so high -- or go even higher. Costs for home repairs have likewise soared, and uncertainty will tend to keep them high. Meanwhile, the general uncertainty about the economy has fueled inflation, leading the Fed to raise rates for the first time in years and to signal that it may raise rates again soon. A result has been 7% mortgages that have pretty much crushed the housing sector. The reduction in construction means fewer homes to insure, and the stagnant resale market limits the opportunities to poach customers as homes change hands. The result will, I believe, be unrelenting pressure on revenue and costs at a time when customers are exhausted from all the post-COVID rate increases. I hope I'm wrong, but it's hard to see a lot of hiring in that sort of environment. Cheers, Paul Image Paul Carroll The latest jobs report for the U.S. highlighted a surprising decline in employment in insurance. I have a theory about the reason -- and it's not AI. items.extracted_text: Supreme Court to Weigh Case Over Race and School Admissions Article 0 Comments The US Supreme Court agreed to consider making it easier to challenge public school admissions policies as racially discriminatory in a fresh test of educational diversity efforts. The justices said Monday they will consider reviving a lawsuit that claims Maryland’s largest school district, Montgomery County, is discriminating against Asian-Americans applicants to its four magnet middle schools. Two lower courts tossed out the suit. Racial-preference opponents are seeking to extend the Supreme Court’s 2023 decision barring universities from using race in admissions for the sake of diversity. That ruling, involving Harvard College and the University of North Carolina, left open questions about policies that affect a school’s racial composition without the explicit consideration of race. The disputed Montgomery County policy puts selected students into an admissions lottery for the magnet schools. The parents fault the school district for using “local norming” to determine which students reach the academic threshold to qualify for the lottery, saying Asian-American students get penalized because they disproportionately attend high-performing, low-poverty elementary schools. The group contends that the 4th US Circuit Court of Appeals applied the wrong legal standard, improperly requiring the parents to show that the system suppresses enrollment of Asian Americans below their share of the applicant pool. The group’s lawyers at Pacific Legal Foundation say they have evidence that officials intentionally discriminated against Asian Americans. “The Constitution protects students as individuals, not as members of a racial group,” Pacific Legal Foundation lawyer Chris Kieser said in a statement. “A school district should not be able to defeat a discrimination claim by showing that its policy did not harm enough Asian-American children.” The parents group, the Association for Education Fairness, sued in 2020 to challenge an earlier policy, which the organization said caused Asian-American admissions to plunge by putting less emphasis on grades and test scores. Montgomery County then adopted the lottery policy for the 2021-22 school year, saying the pandemic made the previous system impossible. The change shifted the focus of the lawsuit to the new policy. The school district urged the Supreme Court not to hear the case, saying the 4th Circuit correctly concluded that the policy doesn’t violate the Constitution’s equal protection clause. Montgomery County says Asian-American students are admitted to the magnet schools at a higher rate than any other racial group. The district also says the parents’ group didn’t point to any statements or conduct suggesting officials intentionally discriminated against Asian Americans. “It is difficult to even conceptualize how a lottery-based admissions policy — adopted in response to an unforeseeable global pandemic — could intentionally discriminate on the basis of race,” the school district said in court papers. The Supreme Court in 2024 turned away similar challenges to admissions policies at elite public high schools in Boston and Fairfax County, Virginia. In each case, conservative Justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito said they would have granted review. Under its normal scheduling practices, the court will hear arguments next year and rule by the end of June. The case is Association for Educational Fairness v. items.extracted_text: Europe EV Sales Rose 70% in September Article 0 Comments Battery-electric vehicle (BEV) registrations in Europe rose 70.3% in September, as high oil prices, subsidies and the availability of more affordable models continue d to lead the growth. Around a third of cars sold across 17 key European markets in September were BEVs, data from E-Mobility Europe, New Automotive and Fier Automotive showed on Monday, amid a deal made by France and Germany to soften proposed EU car emissions rules. BEV registrations reached 300,202 vehicles in September, giving fully electric cars a 32.6% market share 98 million BEVs have been registered across Europe so far this year, up 38.1% from the same period in 2025 France hit a 41.7% BEV market share with 65,243 registrations, while Germany’s share reached 34.6% with 88,724 registrations. The Nordic market remained Europe’s most electrified, led by Norway at 98.8% and followed by Denmark (88.8%), Finland (62.7%) and Sweden (49.0%). BEVs accounted for around half of the registrations in Ireland, Portugal, Belgium and the Netherlands The Czech Republic, Italy and Poland remained among Europe’s least electrified markets at 11.2%, 7.6% and 6.2%, respectively. items.extracted_text: Artemis Monte Carlo Rendezvous Executive Roundtable 2026 - Artemis.bm Artemis Monte Carlo Rendezvous Executive Roundtable 2026 - Artemis.bm Artemis Monte Carlo Rendezvous Executive Roundtable 2026 20th October 2026 - Author: Steve Evans The full report is now available to download from Artemis’ 2026 Monte Carlo Rendezvous Executive Roundtable . The event featured leading insurance-linked securities and reinsurance market experts discussing investor sentiment, market conditions, pricing discipline and emerging opportunities across the catastrophe bond and ILS landscape. Held in September 2026, in partnership with SCOR Investment Partners and Vantage Risk , our sixth ILS-focused roundtable at the annual Monte Carlo reinsurance industry meeting brought together nine market leaders to share their insights and debate the issues shaping the asset class. A full report of the 2026 Artemis Monte Carlo Executive Roundtable event is now available to download for free . Discussions explored evolving investor appetite and sophistication, alongside the importance of continued education and stable pricing as ILS attracts growing interest and continues to mature. The outlook for catastrophe bonds remained positive, with participants highlighting a healthy pipeline for the remainder of 2026 and into early 2027 . Momentum was also viewed as strong across private ILS and blended strategies, underpinned by attractive risk-adjusted returns, diversification, and several years of strong performance. However, as the reinsurance market continues to soften, maintaining underwriting and structural discipline is becoming increasingly important. Participants emphasised the need to remain focused on terms, attachment points and rate adequacy , while questioning whether spreads will stabilise before falling to levels that no longer adequately compensate investors. The discussion also considered opportunities to expand ILS into other areas, including casualty, as well as the potential presented by data centre-related risks. Alongside these opportunities, participants examined what could disrupt the market’s positive trajectory or undermine investor confidence in catastrophe bonds and other ILS structures , even as investor familiarity with and understanding of the asset class continue to deepen. While acknowledging the inherent challenges of predicting market direction, participants anticipated a constructive environment for ILS investors in 2027 . items.title: Car Thefts Are Plunging. Why?
items.original_title: Car Thefts Are Plunging. Why?
items.rss_title: Car Thefts Are Plunging. Why?
items.rss_description: Car Thefts Are Plunging. Why? PaulCarroll Mon, 10/12/2026 - 17:45 The recent report that auto thefts fell 21% in the U.S. in the first half of the year reminds me of a friend's carjacking some 30 years ago — surely the shortest in history. My overeducated friend, with degrees from Brown and the Sorbonne, had just added a certification as an auto mechanic and liked cars that required constant tinkering. While driving near his home in Washington, DC, one afternoon, he stopped at a stop sign, and a pedestrian motioned to him that he had a question. Tim rolled down his window, and the man shoved a gun in his face, ordering him out of the car. The man got in, engaged the clutch and drove... two feet. He tried again, but the car stalled after two more feet. He tried a third time. A fourth. He hadn't even made it halfway into the intersection before he jumped out, threw the keys at Tim's chest and ran off. I'd never thought of having a diseased clutch as an anti-theft device but have watched with interest over the years as actual devices have continually improved. They've now gotten to the point that, combined with other factors, thefts fell 17% in 2024, tumbled 23% last year, to the lowest levels in decades, and are way down again this year. The good news for insurers is likely to continue, too. Let's have a look. Some of my optimism stems simply from the steady modernization of the car fleet. Even though soaring prices for cars have encouraged people to hold on to cars longer than in the past, older, more vulnerable cars are steadily being retired, and that trend will continue. In the face of public pressure, companies whose cars were most likely to be stolen have also issued software patches and other updates — as a result, the percentage of car thefts of Kias and Hyundais fell to 14% of the total last year, from 16% in 2024 and 21% in 2023, even as the total of thefts dropped precipitously. Meanwhile, the supply chain has sorted itself out post-COVID, so thieves can't rack up the sorts of profits they did from stealing scarce parts in recent years. The U.S. war on Iran may unsettle the supply chain again, including by pushing sales of electric vehicles during a time of high gasoline prices, but the effects have been muted so far, and I suspect they'll remain so. Law enforcement has stepped up efforts to prevent all sorts of crimes, and car thefts are a visible target at just about all levels of policing. I'm not sure how much more severe enforcement can become, but, especially in a fraught political environment, I don't see that anyone will relax. Potentially the most important — but fraught — factor that will determine how much car thefts keep falling relates to surveillance technology. Flock has built a massive business by installing cameras on roads nationwide that take pictures of license plates and respond to, among other things, alerts from police departments about stolen vehicles. There are lots of efforts to also figure out how to knit together all the images being gathered by dashcams, which are currently in about one in 10 vehicles in the U.S. and which are being adopted quickly. Combining all those feeds could provide real-time intelligence for police departments, making it far easier to catch thieves and creating a massive disincentive for them to steal cars in the first place. But.... We've also seen how surveillance can be abused, as I wrote in August . Flock faces a scandal because dozens of police officers used its technology to stalk current and former romantic partners, and the temptation to use surveillance illicitly will only increase as the technology becomes more powerful. My gut tells me that it will take time, perhaps years, to sort through all the tensions between law enforcement and privacy but that we'll eventually get to the point where some severely circumscribed uses of license plate readers will take another cut out of auto thefts. The privacy issue is one we've mostly navigated with Ring cameras and surveillance cameras on building, so there's a blueprint for progress The bad guys are always innovating, just as the good guys are, but I think the favorable glide path for car thefts should continue. Cheers, Paul P.S. My other bizarro car theft story, this one involving a nephew and an odd situation for the adjuster: While my nephew was visiting DC last year, his Hyundai was stolen off the street by four kids — who drove the car right past him as he was talking with the police officer who responded to his report of the crime. They took the car on joy rides for a few days — as evidenced by the thousands of dollars of traffic violations they ran up in DC and Maryland — then used it in a drug deal that went bad. The car wound up full of bullet holes, and a friend of the kids was shot. Panicking, the kids put the badly wounded girl in the trunk of the car and dumped her in front of her high school. These young geniuses then abandoned the car and tried to run off but were promptly apprehended by school security. (The girl healed fine.) The insurance issue was that the adjuster couldn't look at the car because it was in police custody as a crime scene. So my nephew's insurer kept him in a rental car for weeks until it finally satisfied itself that the car was a total loss and wrote him a check for a new one. My nephew spent weeks unwinding the traffic tickets. He actually had to drive to Baltimore from Philadelphia to appear in court and provide evidence that he couldn't have been at the wheel for the moving violations because he wasn't in Maryland when they occurred. Image Paul Carroll Car thefts in the U.S. tumbled to their lowest levels in decades in 2025, and are down a further 21% this year. The trend is likely to continue, too. items.rss_title: 3M to Argue Australia’s $1.4 Billion ‘Forever Chemicals’ Lawsuit Legally Flawed
items.rss_description: U.S. conglomerate 3M plans to argue a landmark case brought by Australia over contamination from the company’s use of PFAS “forever chemicals” in its firefighting foam is legally flawed, a court heard on Friday. The claim against the Minnesota-based chemicals …
items.extracted_text: 3M to Argue Australia’s $1.4 Billion ‘Forever Chemicals’ Lawsuit Legally Flawed Article 0 Comments U.S. conglomerate 3M plans to argue a landmark case brought by Australia over contamination from the company’s use of PFAS “forever chemicals” in its firefighting foam is legally flawed, a court heard on Friday. The claim against the Minnesota-based chemicals maker and its local unit is the largest ever brought by Australia, and seeks more than A$2 billion ($1.38 billion) in damages for past and future costs of contamination across 28 military bases where 3M’s products were used. Australia’s case is that 3M knew or ought to have known the foam it made and supplied could damage the environment and harm people, but it failed to warn the government. The foam’s pollution interfered with people’s ability to use and enjoy the water and land around the bases, creating what the government says amounted to a “public nuisance” under Australian law for which 3M should pay compensation. “On Australian authority, the pleaded case does not comprise public nuisance,” 3M’s barrister Philip Solomon said at the first case management hearing for the lawsuit on Friday. “The allegation against us alleged that we, the respondents, had the means to abate the nuisance, that we caused the nuisance, that were responsible for the particular or the special loss associated with the nuisance, and that in a broad sense, we had the ability to control the discharge of the nuisance,” he added. “We will in a number of pages set out why public nuisance as pleaded is not available.” In its defense, expected to be filed on December 11, 3M also plans to question whether another part of Australia’s case — that the company breached consumer protection laws by making misleading claims about the foam’s features and safety — was time-barred because the alleged conduct occurred decades ago, Solomon said. PFAS are a group of manufactured chemicals that are widely used in products resistant to heat, stains, grease and water. Research has linked exposure to PFAS to health issues including liver damage, lower birth weight ⁠and testicular cancer. 3M, which has faced thousands of lawsuits over alleged PFAS contamination, sold the firefighting foam in Australia from 1966 to 2003. Australia has spent A$1.3 billion in dealing with the impacts of the contamination on the bases, including paying A$408 million in legal settlements to affected communities. The defense department has also treated or removed more than 200,000 metric tons ⁠of contaminated soil and treated more than 13 billion liters of water. The case will return to court in December. items.title: Psychological Reactance: The Hidden Bias in Claims Negotiation
items.original_title: Psychological Reactance: The Hidden Bias in Claims Negotiation
items.rss_title: Psychological Reactance: The Hidden Bias in Claims Negotiation
items.rss_description: “Give him a few more dollars and get the file closed.” I do not remember the exact words I used years ago, but I remember the feeling behind them. I was dealing with a claimant attorney who had become one …
items.extracted_text: Psychological Reactance: The Hidden Bias in Claims Negotiation Article 0 Comments “Give him a few more dollars and get the file closed.” I do not remember the exact words I used years ago, but I remember the feeling behind them. I was dealing with a claimant attorney who had become one of those names you recognize before you even finish reading the letter of representation. He could be rude. He would laugh during conversations. On at least one occasion, he hung up on me. Chris Casaleggio The gist of his position was often the same: You know you are going to pay. Eventually, I wanted him gone. The claim was not worth turning into a prolonged battle. A little more money might resolve it, get the release signed and, I hoped, make sure I never had to deal with him again. We settled. Then his name appeared on another claim. And another. Apparently, my strategy had one flaw: He kept getting new clients. Bad luck for me. But looking back, there was a more important lesson. Somewhere in those negotiations, I had stopped evaluating only the claim. How I felt about the person presenting it had entered the equation. That may be one of the biggest negotiation blind spots in claims. The danger is not that adjusters have emotions. We are human. The danger is failing to recognize when emotion starts masquerading as claims judgment. The Urge to Win, and the Urge to Escape Most claims professionals recognize the first version of this problem. An attorney is aggressive. A contractor is confrontational. An insured accuses the carrier of deliberately underpaying. A claimant keeps escalating the same argument. Eventually, the internal dialogue changes. “He’s not going to bully me.” “I’m not giving her another dollar.” “I’m done negotiating.” That is the urge to win. But there is an opposite reaction that may be just as consequential. “Fine. Give them something and close it.” “I just want this file off my desk.” That is the urge to escape. One reaction can make an adjuster more resistant than the facts justify. The other can make an adjuster more accommodating than the facts justify. Both have the same underlying problem: something other than liability, damages, coverage, evidence and exposure has begun influencing the decision. The current claims environment makes this worth examining. The 2026 CLM Litigation Management Study found that 59.4% of carriers reported managing more litigated files than three years earlier, 68.1% reported an increase in attorney-represented claimants and 85.2% reported more policy-limit demands. Perhaps most striking, 96.8% of non-dismissed litigated cases were ultimately resolved through settlement. If negotiation is where so many disputed claims end, understanding what can distort negotiation judgment matters. When Pressure Creates Resistance Psychology gives us language for some of what happens in these moments. One concept is psychological reactance, the tendency to resist when we perceive that someone is threatening our freedom or trying to control our behavior. Researchers conducting a meta-analysis in the January 2026 issue of Human Communication Research found that highly freedom-threatening language produced greater anger, more negative thoughts and greater psychological reactance than less threatening language. Claims professionals do not need a psychology degree to recognize the practical version. “You know you’re going to pay this.” “You have no choice.” “Pay the limits or we’ll see you in court.” Sometimes those statements are legitimate advocacy. Sometimes they are designed to create pressure. But the adjuster’s response can become psychological before it becomes analytical. “No, you are not going to tell me what I have to do.” That is where the blind spot begins. We may believe we are holding firm because the demand is unsupported when part of what we are actually defending is our autonomy. The useful question is simple: Did the facts change, or did my feelings change? When Skepticism Becomes Distrust Claims handling requires skepticism. An adjuster who accepts every allegation, estimate, diagnosis or demand without scrutiny is not doing their job. But skepticism and cynicism are not the same thing. Skepticism asks for proof. Cynicism assumes the answer before the proof arrives. That distinction matters in claims. Experience teaches us to recognize patterns, question inconsistencies and test what we are being told. But after enough inflated demands, questionable invoices, exaggerated presentations and contentious negotiations, healthy skepticism can gradually become something else. A 2026 review in Current Opinion in Psychology examined what researchers call “under-trust” in negotiation. The authors found that negotiators can become overly pessimistic about the honesty of their counterparts. One explanation is that negotiators may assume the other side is driven primarily by self-interest while underestimating the moral considerations that can constrain dishonest behavior. That has an obvious claims application. Experience can begin whispering: “I know how these people operate.” Experience is valuable. Pattern recognition is part of expertise. But a pattern is not proof that the next person fits it. There is a related phenomenon researchers call reactive devaluation. In negotiation, a proposal can appear less attractive simply because it came from the adversary. Experimental negotiation research has demonstrated that who makes a proposal can influence how that proposal is valued. Think about the claims implications. Would the same medical argument seem more persuasive coming from a physician you regularly work with rather than one retained by the claimant? Would an estimate seem more reasonable if it came from a contractor you trusted? Would you react differently to the exact same settlement proposal if it came from an attorney you respected rather than one who had been antagonizing you for six months? That does not mean the sources of information are irrelevant. Credibility matters. History matters. Evidence matters. But so does recognizing when our opinion of the messenger begins affecting our assessment of the message. Confirmation bias can compound the problem. Once we decide an attorney is unreasonable, a contractor inflates everything or a claimant exaggerates, we naturally become more receptive to information confirming that belief and less receptive to evidence contradicting it. The abrasive attorney can still have a valid damages argument. The difficult contractor can still identify something legitimately omitted from an estimate. The angry insured can still raise a coverage issue worth reconsidering. Difficult does not mean wrong. A useful self-check is: If someone I liked and respected presented me with exactly the same information, would I evaluate it differently? If the answer is “Yes,” then personality may have entered the valuation. The Blind Spot Isn’t Limited to Difficult People A recent experience outside of claims made me think about this from another angle. A roofing company caused some minor damage while working at my home, including marks to siding that was already dirty. The existing condition became part of the discussion. The siding was not pristine, so the new marks did not stand out the way they might have on a spotless house. That raised an interesting question. Would identical new damage seem more significant if everything around it had been perfect beforehand? Claims professionals encounter versions of this constantly. The roof was already old. The vehicle already had scratches. The building already had deferred maintenance. The claimant already had a bad back. A preexisting condition absolutely matters. It can affect causation, damages and the proper measure of loss. The goal is not to ignore it. The danger is allowing “It was already imperfect” to quietly become “What happened now matters less.” Consider the bodily injury claim involving someone with years of back problems. “The claimant already had a bad back” may be highly relevant evidence, but it does not answer the entire causation question. What changed after the accident? Were the symptoms more severe? Was there new treatment? New restrictions? An aggravation? Lost time that had not existed previously? Claims rarely involve a blank slate. The danger is allowing what was already wrong to make us undervalue what changed. That is where another concept from behavioral psychology becomes relevant: anchoring (a cognitive shortcut in which people rely too heavily on the first piece of information they get). A 2026 Management Science meta-analysis covering 50 years of anchoring research and more than 2,600 effect sizes concluded that anchoring remains a robust phenomenon in human judgment. That does not mean considering a claimant’s prior injury or a property’s pre-loss condition constitutes anchoring. Those are relevant facts and often essential to the evaluation. It does mean we should remain conscious of how powerfully an initial reference point can influence what comes next. Holding the Line Is Not Bias None of this means an adjuster should become more generous simply because psychological bias exists. Sometimes the demand really is excessive. Sometimes the attorney is applying pressure because the evidence is weak. Sometimes the contractor’s estimate really is inflated. Sometimes the prior medical history explains most of the claimed condition. Sometimes the correct answer is no. items.extracted_text: Clear exit terms and liquid collateral key to lowering casualty sidecar tail risk charges: AM Best - Artemis.bm Clear exit terms and liquid collateral key to lowering casualty sidecar tail risk charges: AM Best - Artemis.bm Clear exit terms and liquid collateral key to lowering casualty sidecar tail risk charges: AM Best 20th October 2026 - Author: Jack Willard As casualty sidecars continue to gain traction, rating agency AM Best has highlighted that clear exit mechanics, high-quality collateral, and transparent risk transfer are critical to lowering tail risk capital charges for sponsors, warning that uncertain exit terms or weak collateral can leave cedents holding unexpected residual risk. In the report, AM Best notes that when a sponsor cedes business to a casualty sidecar, the protection provided by the transaction is limited by the sidecar’s capitalisation, and contractual features such as loss ratio caps. The agency explained that it defines tail risk as the residual exposure borne by the sponsor when sidecar capital is insufficient to absorb losses exceeding expectations, directly influencing how much contingent exposure should reduce the sponsor’s available capital. “Institutional investors, including the private capital involved in establishing these vehicles, generally require a defined path to liquidity. Transactions have started to converge on an exit term of about seven years. Culpeper Capital (one of the lead investors in George Street Re) has pointed to a degree of standardization around that time horizon, since reserves need to be reasonably seasoned before an exit valuation is credible,” said AM Best. The agency importantly states that tail risk matters on both sides of casualty sidecar transactions, given that investors want finality, and cedents want to know what risks (if any), are commuted back to them when an exit is exercised. “The market has now developed a set of exit mechanisms, several of them emerging within the past 24 months. The Forward Exit Option (FEO), established by Enstar, grants investors the right, in exchange for a fee, to novate residual reserves to the legacy specialist under a pricing framework fixed at inception. On exercise, investors receive liquidity and finality, and the option provider assumes the reserve development risk and faces the cedent from that point on. The FEO made its debut in Starwind Specialty’s Fractal Re sidecar, and Enstar has said it is being positioned for broader use, including in property sidecars,” AM Best said. The agency continued: “Scheduled commutations build the exit into the contract from the start Enstar’s Scaur Hill Re, for example, gives investors an optional commutation at year seven and a mandatory exit at year ten, each at pre-specified pricing. After the fact, a loss portfolio transfer (LPT) moves an identified book of reserves to a legacy buyer, an adverse development cover (ADC) absorbs deterioration above a chosen attachment, and secondary sales pass investor interests to incoming investors, though volumes remain modest and pricing stays private.” Turning attention towards QBE Re’s George Street Re casualty sidecar, which was launched at the beginning of the year, AM Best highlighted how this vehicle took a different approach. Instead of attaching an exit option to the structure, the agency noted that it placed legacy specialist Compre inside the investor base from inception alongside Culpeper Capital Partners and Calidris Investment Partners. AM Best added that Compre participates in a defined portion of the George Street Re sidecar, helping shape the contractual terms and the collateral construct that will govern at exit, and is positioned to step into the other investors’ positions over roughly five to seven years, with the ability to take on their future liabilities annually. AM Best further added, “In 2026, Enstar and Artex announced a partnership to embed prospective and retrospective exit solutions across Artex-managed ILS vehicles, an early step toward standardized exit engineering.” Although these mechanisms can provide investors with liquidity or contractual finality, the agency cautioned that they do not eliminate the underlying reserve risk exposure, highlighting that their effect depends on which party retains or assumes that exposure and when any transfer occurs. In addition, AM Best’s report outlines that the float backing these casualty vehicles is commonly invested in credit, which means that just one event, or an inflation spike or credit contraction, can hurt both sides of the vehicle at once, with reserves deteriorating while the collateral behind them loses value. “Hurricane losses do not depend on the state of the economy, and that independence is the basis of the diversification case for traditional property ILS,” AM Best said. Adding: “That linkage between asset values and casualty risk matters directly to AM Best’s tail risk analysis because scenarios in which a sidecar’s capital falls short may also be those in which credit-sensitive collateral is under pressure and the sponsor is less able to absorb the returning risk. The assessment applies stressed correlations between reserve and asset risks and treats illiquid collateral conservatively.” To conclude, AM Best noted that it evaluates exit provisions to determine which party holds the reserve risk exposure after an exit is exercised within these vehicles. “Scheduled commutations imply that reserves may return to the sponsor, so the analysis considers the likely maturity and adequacy of the reserve position at the commutation date. A pre-priced novation to a well-capitalized legacy carrier can genuinely limit the sponsor’s exposure, with the credit given tempered by counterparty strength and the enforceability of the pricing framework,” the report added. AM Best concludes: “Public disclosure of quota-share percentages, collateral guidelines, related-party investment limits, and exit pricing remains limited even as casualty sidecars grow in number and size, and descriptions of three-year underwriting periods do not always make clear that the corresponding investment exposure can continue for considerably longer. Genuine risk transfer, high-quality and liquid collateral, credible reserving, and a clearly defined exit tend to lower the tail risk charge aggressive loss assumptions, poor-quality or illiquid collateral, and uncertain exit provisions tend to raise it.” Find details of numerous reinsurance sidecar investments and transactions, including property, casualty and life reinsurance sidecar structures, in our directory of collateralized reinsurance sidecar transactions . items.extracted_text: Hannover Re sees ILS capital as sustainable reinsurance addition, source of growth: Horstmann - Artemis.bm Hannover Re sees ILS capital as sustainable reinsurance addition, source of growth: Horstmann - Artemis.bm Hannover Re sees ILS capital as sustainable reinsurance addition, source of growth: Horstmann 19th October 2026 - Author: Jack Willard Speaking earlier today during Hannover Re’s Baden-Baden media briefing, Patrick Horstmann Managing Director, and Head of insurance-linked securities (ILS) at the firm, emphasised that the German reinsurer sees ILS capital as a sustainable addition to the global reinsurance market and a key area of growth for the company. Hannover Re has been steadily growing in the ILS market in recent years. In late 2025, the reinsurer launched its Bermuda-based ILS platform, Hannover Re Capital Partners in late 2025, and began writing business at the January 1st 2026 reinsurance renewals to further scale its alternative capital capabilities. “ILS capital has grown over the last years and has also grown relatively more than traditional reinsurance capital. Meanwhile, it’s roughly 18% of the overall reinsurance capacity, and we see alternative capital as a sustainable addition to the traditional capital in the market,” Horstmann explained during the briefing. “Especially in the last year we have seen this increase. But we have seen over the long term and over the long horizon the sustainability of ILS capital in the market,” he continued. Horstmann also outlined that Hannover Re aims to bridge capital markets and cedants, noting that the reinsurer’s ILS activities include five key businesses segments: catastrophe bond transformation, collateralized fronting, life ILS, its cat bond focused manager Leine Investment, and the company’s newest ILS venture the Hannover Re Capital Partners (HCP) unit. “Since November last year, we have launched an insurance agent in Bermuda called Hannover Re Capital Partners, and that is a platform where we connect third-party capital with the risk, utilising our Hannover Re underwriting, modeling, structuring expertise, and so enabling third-party investors to access traditional reinsurance risk with the help of Hannover Re and the support of Hannover Re,” Horstmann added. During the Q&A portion, Horstmann provided more detail on HCP. The executive said the platform is “not a risk-carrying entity” and uses collateralized fronting structures. He also added that HCP has raised a low triple-digit million amount in assets under management and had fully deployed that capital for the July 1st 2026, renewal. “At the moment, we are in discussions with further investors to raise additional capital. But I’m always a bit reluctant to give any aims or targets. What I can say is, we are fully aligned with our business plan, which we had initially. “So we are very satisfied with the development so far and have seen a lot of interest from third-party investors in our activities, appreciating our global market access, our underwriting expertise, and also the ILS knowledge we have gained over the last decades. So we have a lot seen of interest in further discussions,” Horstmann added. In addition, we also asked Horstmann to outline where Hannover Re sees its biggest opportunities in the capital markets and ILS sector for next year? “Focusing on the five pillars we have within ILS at Hannover Re, I would say we have a very good market footprint for catastrophe bond transformation and for the collateralized fronting business. So we expect them in the next year, or the next two years, to be stable, potentially slightly growing,” Horstmann said. Adding: “We have been compared to the market as a bit underrepresented in terms of third-party asset management, so Leine Investment and Hannover Re Capital Partners. So, just because our footprint in the market was not as strong there as for the other areas, I would expect there to be more growth in absolute and on relative terms compared to the other segments.” We also asked Thorsten Steinmann, CEO, E+S Rück, member of the Executive Board, Hannover Re, whether the reinsurer has any plans in place to look at other opportunities to share risk with investor markets in the near future. “We’ve always said in the last few weeks because one of those topics which came up is the topic of casualty sidecars, and this is partially done via Lloyd’s partially directly via investors, and this is a space where we are very cautious and we are not playing in this space. “It’s not part of our product that we are offering to our clients, simply because we believe that the complexity of this long tail business, in combination with the asset management risk that you run, that we are very cautious to play in this field. I’m not saying this is going to be the case forever, but the response today is that we are very cautious and observing,” Steinmann explained. items.extracted_text: Waymo Plans to Quintuple Fleet To 20,000, According to Reports Article 0 Comments Alphabet’s self-driving unit Waymo plans to expand its fleet five-fold to 20,000 by the end of next year using $5 billion it raised earlier this month, Semafor reported on Monday, citing people familiar with the matter. The autonomous ride-hailing service provider, which currently has 4,000 cars, wants to expand it to 8,000 by the end of the year and grow it to 20,000 by the end of next year,Semafor reported Waymo did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment outside regular business hours Waymo secured a $5 billion loan earlier this month from lenders including PIMCO, Blackstone and Sixth Street, and said it will use the funds to expand its services across the US and internationally Waymo operates in 15 US cities and has announced plans to roll out rides in London, Tokyo, Singapore and Canada The company closed a $16 billion equity raise earlier this year at a valuation of $126 billion (Reporting by Ramirez in Mexico City Editing by Diti Pujara) Copyright 2026 Reuters.
